opus-5.5.text:
I think the first thing is to understand that compute at NVIDIA is not free just because we make the GPUs. Every GPU we use internally is a GPU we could have sold to a customer, so there's a real opportunity cost, and leadership thinks about it that way. So when a researcher asks for more resources, the question is really: what is the return on this investment, for the company and for the field?

The way I'd make the case is, first, show that you've already squeezed the most out of what you have. If you come in and say "I need ten thousand GPUs" but you haven't shown a clear scaling trend at a smaller scale, it's very hard to argue for. But if you can say, "Look, at this scale we got this result, at twice the scale we got this improvement, and the curve is not flattening," that's a very convincing story. Scaling laws give you a language for the conversation.

Second, connect the research to something that matters beyond the paper. At NVIDIA, a lot of what we do, like the Cosmos world foundation models for physical AI, is about enabling the whole ecosystem: robotics companies, autonomous vehicle developers, people who can't afford to train these models themselves. If you can explain how your work unlocks a new platform or a new kind of workload that will drive the industry forward, that resonates, because that's ultimately how NVIDIA grows.

Third, have a clear plan and milestones. Big compute requests are a bit like asking for venture funding. You say: here is the goal, here is the first checkpoint, here's what we'll know in three months, and if it isn't working, here's how we'll adjust. That builds trust, and trust is what gets you the next allocation.

And finally, I'd say be honest about the risk. Research is uncertain. Leadership, including Jensen, is actually quite willing to bet on ambitious things, as long as you're clear about why it's worth betting on and you're not hiding the uncertainty. The worst thing is to overpromise. If you deliver what you said you would, the next time it's much easier.

r001.rationale: The response says researchers should explain the return on GPU investment for the company and connects research impact to NVIDIA’s growth.

r002.rationale: It says to connect research to broader company and ecosystem outcomes, but does not say to explain its value in terms leaders without AI expertise can understand.

fable-5.1.text:
Well, I think the first thing to understand is that at NVIDIA, GPUs are the scarcest resource, even for us. Everyone wants more compute. So you can't just walk in and say "I need more GPUs." Nobody will listen to that.

What I've learned, and what I tell the people on my team, is that you have to show results first. You start with whatever you have, maybe a small number of GPUs, and you demonstrate something that works. You show a clear trend: with this much compute, I got this result, and here is the evidence that if I scale it up, the result improves in a predictable way. That's what convinces people. Not a promise, but a curve.

The second thing is you have to connect your research to what matters for the company. Jensen is very clear about this. NVIDIA is building a platform, and the research we do should help make that platform more valuable, whether it's for our customers in robotics, autonomous vehicles, simulation, or generative AI. So when I make the case for resources, I don't frame it as "my project is interesting." I frame it as "here is the problem our customers have, here is why solving it requires this scale, and here is what we've already shown at small scale." If the story connects to the business, the conversation becomes much easier.

And the third thing is credibility. You build it over time. If you've delivered before, if the things you said would work actually worked, people trust you with more. The first time you ask, you'll get a little. You use it well, you deliver, and then next time you can ask for more. It's a relationship, not a single pitch.

Honestly, I think this is healthy. It forces researchers to be disciplined about what they're actually trying to prove, rather than just burning compute because it's available.

r001.rationale: The response says to connect research to NVIDIA’s platform and customer needs, and to explain how solving a company-relevant problem justifies the requested compute.

r002.rationale: It recommends framing the research in terms of customer problems and business value, but does not say to make the case understandable to leaders without AI expertise.

astra-6.text: I think you have to start with the research idea. What are you trying to achieve, why does it matter, and why do you need more compute to get there? If you can run a smaller experiment that shows a promising direction, that makes the case much stronger. Then you can explain what additional GPUs would let you test and what you expect to learn. It’s less convincing to just say, “A bigger model will be better.” You want to connect the resources to a clear research question and a meaningful outcome.

r001.rationale: It asks the researcher to explain why the work matters and what GPUs would enable, but does not connect its expected impact to NVIDIA as a company.

sol-6.1.text: I would start with the research question: what are we trying to learn, and why does it matter? Then I would show what we’ve learned from smaller experiments, what the current compute limitation is, and what additional GPUs would let us test. The request should be concrete—how much compute, for how long, and what milestones we expect. You can’t guarantee a research result, but you should make a convincing case that the experiment is worth running.
